draft.title: Mass and the effect of a force
card: Mass is the amount of matter in an object. A heavy object has more mass than a light one.
If the same force is applied to a light object and a heavy one, the light object changes its motion more. It speeds up, slows down or turns by a bigger amount.
A heavier object resists changes to its motion more. It needs a bigger force to start moving or to stop.
For example, a shopping trolley that is empty is easy to get moving and easy to stop. The same trolley full of groceries needs a bigger push to start and a bigger force to stop.
draft.remember: The more mass an object has, the more force it needs to change its motion.

a.q: Two students give a football and a bowling ball the same kick. Which result is expected?
opts: The football speeds up more than the bowling ball
The bowling ball speeds up more than the football
Both speed up by exactly the same amount
Only the football moves, as the bowling ball stays still
a.why: The football has less mass, so the same kick changes its motion more. The bowling ball is tempting because it is heavier, but a heavier object changes its motion less for the same force.

b.q: Jess pushes an empty wheelie bin along her driveway in Hobart. She then fills it with bricks and wants to stop it rolling at the same speed. What is needed?
opts: A bigger force, because the bin now has more mass
A smaller force, because the bin is now heavier
The same force, because the speed has not changed
No force, because the bin will stop by itself
b.why: The full bin has more mass, so it resists changes to its motion more. A bigger force is needed to stop it. The same force option is tempting because the speed is the same, but the mass is not.
b.clue: Think about what filling the bin with bricks changes.

a.best: The football speeds up more than the bowling ball

b.best: A bigger force, because the bin now has more mass

problems.detail: 'wants to stop it rolling at the same speed' is awkward and can be misread as wanting it to stop rolling at a steady speed. Clearer: 'It is now rolling at the same speed as before. What force is needed to stop it in the same distance?' Adding the same distance or time also removes the loophole that a smaller force applied for longer could stop it.

check.summary: The card, the remember line and question a are accurate and suit Year 7. Question b's stem is awkwardly worded and should say the bin is rolling at the same speed as before and must stop in the same distance.
